newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan beer makers take their battle to Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: Japan beer makers take their battle to Taiwan.

text.p: Japan's top breweries have dramatically boosted their exports to Taiwan in recent years and are now poised to grab a bigger slice as Taipei prepares to further open its market to foreign beer makers.

Not content with booming exports, Japan's three largest beer makers -- Kirin Brewery Co Ltd, Asahi Breweries Ltd and Sapporo Breweries Ltd -- now want to take it one step further by producing their beer locally.
The Taiwanese government is expected to allow foreign companies to begin local production as early as the beginning of 1997 as part of its deregulation policy, Japanese brewery officials said.
Already, Sapporo Breweries has said it has agreed with Taiwan's Dong Hsun Hsin Trading Co Ltd to set up an equally owned joint venture to produce Sapporo beer starting in 1999.

The total investment in the project is expected to reach 12 billion yen ($108 million). The joint venture's production facility, due to be built in central Taiwan, will initially have an annual capacity of 100,000 kilolitres, a Sapporo spokesman said.

"Local production has certain advantages such as the freshness of products and a significant reduction in the shipment cost, which will strengthen our competitiveness against local products," said the spokesman.
A spokesman for Japan's largest beer maker, Kirin Brewery, said the company was also actively seeking a partner to produce locally in Taiwan.
"Taiwan's market appears very promising for foreign beer makers. Sales of foreign brands have been growing rapidly since the government allowed beer imports in 1988," he said.
Kirin expects to export 17,000 kilolitres (kl) of its beer to Taiwan in 1996, up from 10,500 kl in 1995. Just two years ago, the company was exporting only 3,400 kl to the island.
Sapporo, which is a strong Japanese rival of Kirin's in Taiwan, expects to boost its exports to 5,700 kl in 1996, up from 5,000 kl in 1995.
Japan's number two, Asahi, which began beer exports to Taiwan in April 1995, has seen a 30 percent year-on-year rise in exports so far this year, a spokesman said.
While the beer makers can expect to count on Taiwan's strong economic fundamentals and growing middle class to help them, politics may blur the overall rosy picture.
A recent row between Japan, Taiwan and China over ownership of a chain of islands in the East China Sea casts a dark cloud over the Japanese beer makers' expansion plans.
Already, the dispute has led to measures to block Japanese firms from bidding for contracts in one major Taiwanese county.

However, spokesmen for the companies said it is still too early to determine whether or not the dispute will prompt the Taiwanese government to put into place measures to hamper Japanese beer makers' entry.
Japanese beer makers are also rushing to tap into the Chinese market, now the world's second largest.
Total beer consumption in China was around 14 million kl in 1994, second only to the United States, and is expected to reach 20 million kl by around 2000, the Kirin spokesman said.
Kirin has licensed 15 factories in China to produce its beer since May 1995. Asahi hopes to locally make its mainstay brand, Super Dry, in China as early as the end of next year.
Sapporo plans to launch a joint venture with Marubeni Corp and two Chinese beer makers to start producing Sapporo beer in China next year, the company spokesman said. ($1=111 yen)
